body.head: Theatrical Examiner.
body.p: The reader, who is familiar with the nonsense and stale wretchedness of the modern drama, and has seen it beginning to meet with universal contempt, would hardly imagine that another author,-a Mr. Burton, it is said,-should start up to give us the same plot and the same characters that we have witnessed a thousand times; and still less would he imagine, that the said Mr. Burton should flatter himself that such plots and characters were new. Yet a gentleman so inexperienced has just arisen; and in a piece called Right and Wrong, which was performed here last Thursday, has told us the old story of a wicked relation, who forges a will, and how the young man, who has a right to the estate, comes home from sea, and how he finds his sweetheart courted by the wicked relation, who forges a will,-and how the young man, as has a right to the estate, comes from from sea, and how he fidns his sweetheart courted by the wicked relation, but she won't listen to him:-futhermore, how this wicked relation, not content with courting the wronged young man's sweetheart, courts his sister too with unlawful purposes, but is prevented therein by her faithful love; and how an old farmer refuses to enter into the wicked relation's desigus; and how, at last, the accomplice in his wickedness, not being satisfied with the money he gets out of him, turns against him, and discovers all; upon which the posession of the great, big estate is restored to the lawful owner, and the wicked man is punished, and the good young men and their sweethearts are all made happy after;-thereby showing, to the satisfaction fo all those who run on in unlawful doings, and never think of their latter end, how Virtue is sure to be rewarded at last, while Vice, though it seems to flourish for a time, yet by the inscrutable ways of Providence, which nobody can find them out, is suddenly brought to nothing and vanisheth, as it were, into nonght. The other characters, not mentioned in this sketch, are an old gentleman, who prefers money, as usual, to the young folks' happpiness,-a foppish servant, who affects Bond-street and is as stupid as he wishes,-and a young rustic, who is fond of fine words and makes blunders like Mrs. Shipslop:-and with this plot and these characters, accompanied by teh most common-place dialogue, the author really seems to imagine that he has done something creditable and original, for in the epilogue he mentions as a sort of joke, that the vile critics will call them old and allow him no merit. It is well that he can think so pleasantly on the subject, though the reception of the play must have rather lessened his vivacity, since with due allowance for those happy persons who are always willing to be pleased with nonsense, and to shew their good nature at the expense of their judgment, the piece was well hissed during the two last acts and most obstreperously damned at the conclusion. So much for Right and Wrong.

The Christmas pantomimes go off very well altogether. The clown at this theatre is a very good one, and though he talks too much and is not so inventive in his tricks as Grimaldi, is no mean rival of him in point of dislocating his limbs and making a piece of India-rubber of himself. The machinery does not second the exertions of Harlequin; the transformations have a knack of stopping half way like Ovid's Metamorphoses in a picture; and the houses, that are struck out of posts and pictures, sometimes stand lugging up an unfinished piece of themselves, like a person who cannot get his watch out of his fob. It would be as well too if the Manager, in selecting his Fairy Tale, would pitch upon one that had no ladies with cats' heads in it: the surprise when they lift up their veils may amuse the children; but it is disagreeable, and perhaps dangerous to grown females under certain circumstances.

As to the elephant at Covent Garden, who is young and sprightly, he seems to have a better taste than his employers, and is so impatient of appearing on the stage, that curiosity is rather baulked than gratified. Perhaps all those who go in the hope of seeing him, are not aware that elephants are subject to sudden fits of rage, and have no natural forbearance in favour of theatrical amateurs. It would not be matter of surprise, if some serious accident, arising from the foolish, and indeed inhuman, introduction of animals on the stage, should put an end to it for ever one of these days.
